section.title: A Brief History
section.p: Indexeshistory of Alexandrian Library Indexes have been around for nearly as long as the written word. As soon as a store of knowledge became too great to hold in one’s brain, then an index, or “pointer” to the information, was needed. The great Greek Alexandrian Library contained more than 400,000 written scrolls. Imagine the time it would take to unroll each scroll in turn to find the information you needed.

Later, when the codex, or book form, developed, guides to a book’s contents, called either an “index” or a “table,” were created. After the invention of printing, when it was possible to create multiple identical copies of a text, indexes came into their own.

section.title: Purposes: What Do Indexes Do?
section.p: Collocation Indexespurposes of Indexes provide access to information. They do this by collecting together in one place similar concepts from disparate sections of the text (a process called “collocation”). The terms representing the various collected concepts are then presented to the user in a known or stated searchable order.
It is important to note that the purpose of the index is not to repeat information in the text, but merely to point the user to it.

section.title: Business Context
section.p: Business context for indexes Cambridge Dictionary of American BiographyCambridge Dictionary of American Biography Oxford Dictionary of QuotationsOxford Dictionary of Quotations Why is this index being created? What purpose will it serve? Is it a marketing tool? One reference book, Cambridge Dictionary of American Biography (1995), boasts of its indexes on the back cover. In the Oxford Dictionary of Quotations (1999), the index comprises 27 percent of the total length of the book, demonstrating its importance for users.

Reader’s Guide to Periodical LiteratureReaders Guide to Periodical Literature Serving as an index may be the sole purpose of a publication. Think of the Reader’s Guide to Periodical Literature, for example. The index is the book, whose sole raison d’être is to direct readers to primary source material.

section.title: Index Users
section.p: Userstypes of Known-item finding Generally, there are two types of users that indexers must keep in mind:

ol.li: People who have not read the book, but are perusing the index before they buy it to find out what kinds of information it contains
Those who have previously read the book and are consulting the index to find something they know they had seen in the text (called “known-item finding”)

section.p: Concordances There are occasions when each word in a text is indexed; such word listings are known as concordances. The Bible and Shakespeare’s works have often had concordances prepared for them. A concordance, however, is not a subject index; it is merely a list of terms like nouns, adjectives, and verbs.

section.title: Content
section.p: Contentas context for index ContentTexts What is the nature of the specific material being indexed? Is it a short guidebook or a thousand-page graduate textbook? A software manual with a limited shelf life? Reference material? Fiction? (Yes, fiction is sometimes indexed.) A multivolume encyclopedia?

Controlled vocabulary If millions of documents are being retrospectively indexed for inclusion in an enterprise-wide content management system, then you may need to develop a controlled vocabulary for use with an automatic indexing tool.
